{{Short description|Numbers in a type of Lucas sequence}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Jacobsthal numbers''' are an [[integer sequence]] named after the [[Germany|German]] mathematician [[Ernst Jacobsthal]].  Like the related [[Fibonacci number]]s, they are a specific type of [[Lucas sequence]] <math>U_n(P,Q)</math> for which ''P''&nbsp;=&thinsp;1, and ''Q''&nbsp;=&nbsp;&minus;2<ref name="mathworld">{{MathWorld |urlname=JacobsthalNumber |title = Jacobsthal Number}}</ref>—and are defined by a similar [[recurrence relation]]: in simple terms, the sequence starts with 0 and 1, then each following number is found by adding the number before it to twice the number before that.  The first Jacobsthal numbers are:

:[[0 (number)|0]], [[1 (number)|1]], 1, [[3 (number)|3]], [[5 (number)|5]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[21 (number)|21]], [[43 (number)|43]], [[85 (number)|85]], [[171 (number)|171]], 341, 683, 1365, 2731, 5461, 10923, 21845, 43691, 87381, 174763, 349525, … {{OEIS|id=A001045}}

A '''Jacobsthal prime''' is a '''Jacobsthal number''' that is also [[prime number|prime]]. The first Jacobsthal primes are:

:3, 5, 11, 43, 683, 2731, 43691, 174763, 2796203, 715827883, 2932031007403, 768614336404564651, 201487636602438195784363, 845100400152152934331135470251, 56713727820156410577229101238628035243, … {{OEIS|id=A049883}}

== Jacobsthal numbers ==

Jacobsthal numbers are defined by the recurrence relation:

:<math>J_n = \begin{cases}
0                  & \mbox{if } n = 0; \\
1                  & \mbox{if } n = 1; \\
J_{n-1} + 2J_{n-2} & \mbox{if } n > 1. \\
\end{cases}</math>

The next Jacobsthal number is also given by the recursion formula

: <math>J_{n+1} = 2J_n + (-1)^n,</math>

or by

: <math>J_{n+1} = 2^n - J_n.</math>

The second recursion formula above is also satisfied by the [[powers of 2]].

The Jacobsthal number at a specific point in the sequence may be calculated directly using the closed-form equation:<ref name="oeis_jl" />

:<math>J_n = \frac{2^n - (-1)^n}{3}.</math>
The [[generating function]] for the Jacobsthal numbers is

:<math>\frac{x}{(1+x)(1-2x)}.</math>

The sum of the [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocals]] of the Jacobsthal numbers is approximately 2.7186, slightly larger than [[e (mathematical constant)|e]].

The Jacobsthal numbers can be extended to negative indices using the recurrence relation or the explicit formula, giving

:<math>J_{-n} = (-1)^{n+1} J_n / 2^n</math> (see {{OEIS2C|id=A077925}})

The following identities holds

:<math>2^n(J_{-n} + J_n) = 3 J_n^2 </math> (see {{OEIS2C|id=A139818}})

:<math>J_n = F_n + \sum_{i=0}^{n-2}J_iF_{n-i-1} </math> where <math>F_n</math> is the ''nth'' Fibonacci number.

== Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers ==

Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers represent the complementary Lucas sequence <math>V_n(1,-2)</math>. They satisfy the same recurrence relation as Jacobsthal numbers but have different initial values: 

:<math> 
  j_n =  
    \begin{cases}
      2                     & \mbox{if } n = 0; \\
      1                     & \mbox{if } n = 1; \\
      j_{n-1} + 2j_{n-2}    & \mbox{if } n > 1. \\
    \end{cases}
</math>

The following Jacobsthal–Lucas number also satisfies:<ref name="oeis_jl">{{Cite OEIS|sequencenumber=A014551|name=Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers}}</ref>

:<math>
  j_{n+1} = 2j_n - 3(-1)^n. \,
</math>

The Jacobsthal–Lucas number at a specific point in the sequence may be calculated directly using the closed-form equation:<ref name="oeis_jl" />

:<math>
  j_n = 2^n + (-1)^n. \,
</math>

The first Jacobsthal–Lucas numbers are:

:[[2 (number)|2]], [[1 (number)|1]], [[5 (number)|5]], [[7 (number)|7]], [[17 (number)|17]], [[31 (number)|31]], [[65 (number)|65]], [[127 (number)|127]], [[257 (number)|257]], [[511 (number)|511]], 1025, 2047, 4097, [[8191 (number)|8191]], 16385, 32767, [[65,537|65537]], 131071, 262145, 524287, 1048577, … {{OEIS|id=A014551}}.

== Jacobsthal Oblong numbers ==

The first Jacobsthal Oblong numbers are: 
0, 1, 3, 15, 55, 231, 903, 3655, 14535, 58311, … {{OEIS|id=A084175}}

:<math>Jo_{n} = J_{n} J_{n+1}</math>
